newsitem.title: POLAND: Poland on track, not complacent - World Bank chief.
newsitem.headline: Poland on track, not complacent - World Bank chief.

text.p: World Bank President James Wolfensohn praised Poland on Friday for its lack of complacency despite its strong economic growth and offered it extensive loans and advice to help key reforms on the way to EU entry.
But recognising Poland may not call for large credits, he told a news conference: "We have absolutely no desire to force money down the throat of the Polish government."

"I have been reconfirmed in my view that current financial management of the country is on track and I was pleased to see, at all levels, no sense of complacency but a real sense of seeking to manage the economy and keep it within appropriate limits," Wolfensohn said after talks with Polish leaders.

The bank this month agreed with Warsaw a country assistance programme naming several projects for which between $200 million and $400 million a year in credits would be available until the year 2000. @
The Bank's Warsaw representative Paul Knotter said earlier this week the bank's approach in Poland would shift focus from lending to guarantees, technical assistance and advice.
Such guarantees could be applied to motorway building, power generation and municipal infrastructure projects.
Between 1990, the year after the fall of communism, and 1996, World Bank loans to Poland totalled $4.1 billion.
Wolfenshohn has held talks with Poland's President, Prime Minister and Finance Minister since arriving on Wednesday for a five-day official visit.
He said that on Friday he met central bank chief Hanna Gronkiewicz-Waltz, who said cutting inflation was a central element of policy and economic overheating was to be avoided.

The bank's central Europe economist Luca Barbone signalled concern over whether savings and investment were high enough to sustain Poland's fast growth to reduce the gap with existing members of the EU, which Poland hopes to join by around 2002.

"We do think the rate of savings and investment in Poland is still low relative to what needed to sustain growth of six or seven percent a year over a period of 10-15 years, which is what you need to get to levels of per capita income of the EU," he told the news conference.
Wolfensohn said the bank aimed to help sustain growth, promote private enterprise and reform of the financial sector.
Especially important was helping to sustain reforms in the social sector, in pensions, social security and education.
He said Poland's switch from the current hugely expensive and inefficient pension system, launched this year with three bills creating a new pension funds structure, had to continue.
"In that transition it is possible...the bank may be asked to provide some financial role and, if it is, we will be happy to do it," he said.
He said there was no immediate need for another financial sector adjustment loan from the bank for Poland.

The bank was working to deepen the financial system through the private sector and advice to government, strengthening banks and establishing leasing companies, and trying to develop mechanisms to help small to medium firms, he added.
He said the bank would also offer to help fund retraining and regional development for miners laid off in a continuing programme of restructuring the coal industry.
